Average reward adjusted discounted reinforcement learning
Manuel Schneckenreither1 • Georg Moser2
Received: 17 November 2022 / Accepted: 4 October 2024 / Published online: 18 January 2025  The Author(s) 2025
Abstract In this paper, we provide a novel view upon reinforcement learning (RL for short). In particular, we are interested in applications of RL in use cases, where average rewards may be nonzero. While RL methodologies have been extensively researched upon, this particular application area has only received scarce attention in the Literature. In part, our motivation stems from applications in Operation Research (OR for short), where it is typically the case that rewards are profit derived. Similar use cases can be found in more general applications in economics. Based on a principled study of the mathematical background of discounted reinforcement learning we establish a novel adaptation of standard RL, dubbed Average Reward Adjusted Discounted Reinforcement Learning (ARAL for short). Our approach stems from revisiting the Laurent Series expansion of the discounted state value and a subsequent reformulation of the target function guiding the learning process. While the theoretical advance is arguably incremental, we provide ample experimental evidence that the thus obtained novel RL methodology compares favorable to well-established techniques like Q-learning or R-learning.
Keywords Machine learning  Reinforcement learning  Average reward learning  Operations research  Applications
1 Introduction
Due to its generality Reinforcement Learning (RL for short) methodologies have been investigated in many application areas and RL has seen astonishing success in many such areas. We are concerned with an adaption of standard discounted reinforcement learning. The motivation for this study—in part—stems from our interest in applications in Operation Research (OR for short), where it is typically the case that in general rewards are positive. Similar use cases can be found in more general applications in Economics. In such cases the average rewards of the agent’s actions may be nonzero. While RL methodologies have been
extensively researched upon, this particular application area has only received scarce attention in the Literature.
To wit, RL is most often applied to control problems, games and other sequential decision-making tasks, where—historically— in almost all steps the reward function returns 0, cf. [1].1 Sometimes also a fixed constant value, e.g. 1, is used as reward in every step, resulting in the inability of improving the policy by optimizing the average reward.
Hence, we focus on application areas and use cases that produce an average reward per step that cannot be approximated by 0. Based on a principled study of the mathematical background of discounted reinforcement learning we establish a novel adaptation of standard RL, dubbed Average Reward Adjusted Discounted Reinforce- ment Learning (ARAL for short). Consider the Laurent Series expansion of the discounted state value. When the discounted state values are decom- posed into its subcomponents, one can see that the state values are, to an extensive amount, composed of the average reward-term, while the other terms appear mar- ginal. This results from the fact that, in contrast to the other terms, the average reward is exponentially scaled by an inverse magnitude of the chosen discount factor and that, for most applications, the average reward is equal among all states. Now, if the average reward is nonzero, due to the iterative nature of RL, the agent cannot distinguish between actions, as in the learning phase all actions seem to be equally good, which may result in suboptimal policies.
We argue that this is the primal reason that discounted RL is inappropriate for these kinds of applications. Earlier, this has already been emphasized by Schwartz and Mahadevan. In [3] Schwartz introduced a novel approach to RL, dubbed R-learning, as partial remedy to this prob- lem. Further, based on [3], Mahadevan provided a princi- pled study of average reward reinforcement learning (see. [4–8]).
Our contribution aims at a combination discounted and average reward RL, to get the best parts of both worlds. On the one side, the stability and simplicity of standard dis- counted RL. On the other side, the idea of assessing the average reward separately and, with that, aiming for broader optimality criteria of average reward RL. More precisely, we make the following contributions.
1. First we analyze and illustrate why standard discounted RL is inappropriate in use case, where the average reward that cannot be approximated with 0. 2. Second, we establish ARAL, as a novel near-Black- well-optimal RL algorithm and analytically prove its optimality. 3. Third, we provide ample experimental validation of ARAL. In particular, we provide ample evidence for ARAL competitiveness in relation to Q-learning and R-learning methodologies. ARAL is shown to perform well on various benchmark problems, including a well- studied M/M/1 admission control queuing system and classic-control RL environments. It outperforms the other methodologies in most tasks, reduces the number of learning steps in comparison to Q-Learning and, in contrast to R-Learning, performs very stable. The experiment results further show that it performs well over a wide range of parameterisations. Finally, it learns sensible policies for all tested RL environments of different complexities.
Arguably our observations on the Laurent series expansion and thus the theoretical foundations of ARAL are quite straightforward. In particular, when presented in relation to the seminal studies of Schwartz and Mahadevan. However, quite surprisingly ARAL compares favorable to well- established techniques like Q-learning. Further, we can validate improvements over existing dedicated approaches on average reward RL, like R-learning.
Application areas of our methodology—taking inspira- tion from use cases in OR or economics is general—could be (i) an agent that periodically decides on buying and selling instruments at the stock market; (ii) an agent per- forming daily replenishment decisions; or (iii) many other decision problems that arise in hierarchical supply chain and production planning systems, which are strongly capacity-oriented [9] and with aggregated feedback (see for example [10–12]).
We emphasize that the experimentally validated improvements of ARAL, cf. Sect. 8, are solely based on a principled study of the Laurent series expansion in partic- ular and standard discounted RL methodologies, in general. Our novel methodology achieves non-trivial improvements over well-established techniques (e.g. Q-learning or R-learning), without the incorporation of sophisticated extensions. Thus, ARAL constitutes an effective reformu- lation of existing methodology, which can be implemented rather efficiently.
1.1 Structure
The rest of the paper is structured as follows. The next section provides a high-level overview of ARAL. Section 3 discusses related work, while Sect. 4 established founda- tions of ARAL and fixes notations. In particular, we recall the Laurent series expansion of discounted state values in this section. Section 5 identifies issues with discounted and average reward RL in our context. Section 6 details the methodology of ARAL, while Sects. 7 and 8 detail the benchmarks and provide experimental evaluations of our algorithm, respectively. Finally, we conclude in Sect. 9.

2.2 ARAL algorithm
Our approach estimates the average reward value and uses average reward adjusted discounted state values to be able to selectively choose the best actions. In particular, ARAL infers
1. the average reward, computed based on the state values of consecutively observed states and the returned reward (in contrast to exponentially smooth- ing observed reward signals); 2. approximates the bias values; and 3. uses a smaller discount factor to infer the error term values.
Thus, in addition to the average reward ARAL employs (i) the bias value and (ii) the error term.
Intuitively, the bias value describes the collected reward that is additionally received together with the average reward, when starting in a specific state. The error term incorporates in which step and to what extent the bias value is collected (see Sect. 4 for the mathematical definitions). Being not only a measure of extent, but also one of time
(steps), the error term only exists for discount factors strictly less than 1, hence, the name.
Despite the name ‘‘error term’’, there exists an intrinsic objective of maximizing the error term. A higher value signifies to collect the full amount of the bias value earlier. Consider an agent that either expects to have infinitely much time to collect rewards or one that is unaware when the system will halt. Then the most sensible approach is to first select actions that return the highest average reward. Second, chose those that return the highest bias value. Third, consider when and to what extent the additional reward, i.e. the bias value, is collected. The latter is equivalent to maximizing the error term. A policy that collects the highest possible average reward is referred to as gain-optimal. A gain-optimal policy that collects the highest possible bias value is called bias-optimal.
Hence, in ARAL the actions are chosen by, first, col- lecting as much reward as possible by aiming for bias- optimality (and therefore also gain-optimality), and, only afterward, by considering paths that collect the additional reward earlier. We will see, cf. Section 5, that in general policies inferred by Q-Learning are neither bias-optimal, nor gain-optimal.

3 Related work
In the following, for brevity, we focus on related work that primarily focus on average reward. Similarly, we exclude applications that use continuous action spaces, as they are out of the scope of this paper. (In future work we will seek extensions of ARAL to this avail). In order to structure related work, we explicitly distinguish between (i) the standard discounted framework [20, 142ff]; (ii) the aver- age reward framework [20, 331ff]; and finally (iii) our - ARAL framework, as a mixture of both.
3.1 Related work in operations research/robotics
Only a very limited number of OR optimisation papers that use RL wrt. average reward problems are available. In [21], the first author and Haeussler present an RL algorithm, which optimizes order release decisions in production control environments. They use sophisticated additions to allow the agent to link the actions to the actual rewards. The results were compared to static order release measures only, which were outperformed.
Gijsbrechts et al. [22] apply RL on a dual sourcing problem for replenishment of a distribution center using rail or road, and compare their results to optimal solutions
if tractable or otherwise established heuristics. They found that hyperparameter tuning is effort-intensive and the resulting policies are often not optimal, especially for lar- ger problems.
Balaji et al. [23] use out-of-the-box RL algorithms with simple 2 layer neural networks to tackle stochastic bin packing, newsvendor and vehicle routing problems (VRP). VRP is a generalized travelling salesperson problem (TSP), where one or more vehicles have to visit nodes in a graph. They report to sometimes beat the benchmarks and find sensible solutions.
The capacitated VRP is also tackled with RL by Nazari et al. [24]. They minimize the total route length and compare the results to optimal solutions for small instan- ces. Although the optimum is not reached, one instance, which keeps track of the most probable paths, performs better than well-established heuristics. Also for larger problem sizes this technique seems to outperform the other tested methods. Vera and Abad [25] extend this model to a multi-agent algorithm and thus tackle the capacitated multi-vehicle routing problem with a fixed fleet size. They also report better results compared to the heuristics, espe- cially for large problem sizes, but in contrast to [24] are outperformed by Google’s OR-Tools.4 These applications, like other TSP applications, e.g. [26, 27], of RL to the VRP, except for [23], however, calculate the reward according to the length to the finished route, while returning reward 0 during the path creation. Thus, the average reward for long routes can be approximated with 0 as the decision problem is episodic and therefore perform well.
Finally, there are applications to the beer distribution game [28, 29], but the problem sizes and thus complexities are small. Further, only small problem sizes are handled or far-from-optimal solutions are reported. All of the above cited papers use highly sophisticated methods (e.g. actor- critic RL methods, which not only learn a value function, but explicitly model the policy), but conceptually remain routed in (standard) discounted RL framework.
In recent years the number of publications in specific areas of Operations Research and Robotics, as for instance in Autonomous Multi-Vehicle Systems [30], has increased exponentially.
3.2 Extensions of reinforcement learning
Drawbacks of standard discount reinforcement learning led the way to the development of multi-period sampling approaches, most prominently n-step learning, as, for instance, in A3C [17], and, especially, Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) [2].

PPO is an actor-critic policy gradient method, enrooted in Trust Region Policy Optimisation and actor-critic RL, that learns from its interaction with the environment. The policy (actor) and state-action function (critic) are repre- sented by an artificial neural network (ANN) while parallel agents gather multiple consecutive experiences of the environment before each update, similar to n-step Q- Learning [17, 31]. While average rewards problems are not in the focus of PPO, we hypothesize that its sophistication would allow better results in this context, too. This yields from the fact that PPO is not safe from shifting the state values, as it does not model the average reward separately and does not distinguish between greedy and non-greedy actions during learning. The latter is known to introduce inaccuracies [32]. This hypothesis is supported by the results of Average Policy Optimisation, a trust region approach with average reward [33]. For most tasks of the continuous control environments of MuJoCo it outperforms PPO. Other noteworthy and sufficiently recent develop- ments of RL are Soft Actor-Critic is a stable off-policy actor-critic deep RL algorithm based on the maximum entropy reinforcement learning framework [34], and DreamerV3 [35], which is a recent actor-critic RL method that infers world models using auto-encoders. For further development of extension of reinforcement learning we refer to [36].
3.3 Average reward learning
A different approach, extensively studied in the Literature, is Average Reward RL, where no discount factor is used but rather nested constraint problems are approximated iteratively. The latter immediately leads to computational intensive calculations. Mahadevan [4] establish mainly foundations and examine R-Learning, an Average Reward RL algorithm. R-learning was proposed by Schwartz [15], but is generally not sophisticated enough to produce bias- optimal policies (see Sect. 4 for the definitions of bias value and bias-optimality). Then, RL optimality criteria are thoroughly discussed by Mahadevan [5], while in [6, 7] model-based and model-free bias-optimal algorithms are presented. The main issue with the algorithms of [6, 7] is, that the derivation that is generated in the last constraint level, is simply ignored. We implemented the algorithm of [7] and observed suboptimal policies. Similarly, Tadepalli
and Ok [37] present a model-based Average Reward RL algorithm, called H-Learning, which under certain assumptions finds bias-optimal values. Furthermore, they apply it to simulated automatic guided vehicle scheduling. Additionally, they observed that the average reward has to be updated by line two in Eq. 2 and not by exponentially smoothing the actual observed rewards. The latter is done in the algorithms of [6, 7], which increases the probability of finding suboptimal policies, as the state-action update values lack behind, by being computed using a lagged average reward estimate, in contrast to a prediction based on the received reward and current state values estimations (cf. line 2 in Eq. 2). Later, Mahadevan et al. [8] lift the model-free average reward RL algorithm to continuous- time semi-Markov Decision Processes (semi-MDPs), which handle non-periodic decision problems, and apply it to an inventory problem consisting of a single machine. The algorithm of Mahadevan et al. [8], called SMART, was applied on the optimisation of transfer lines using a hier- archical approach [38] and preventive maintenance of a production inventory system [39]. Although the results are promising, the adaption to continuous-time problems eases the complexity for most applications. However, in practice usually decision have to be made on a daily basis [40]. Therefore, we refrain from this adaption and concentrate on standard MDPs only. Furthermore, often continuous-time semi-MDP problems can be converted through uniformi- sation into equivalent discrete time instances, cf. [20, 41].
There are various other approaches on average reward RL, like RVI Q-Learning [42], GR-Learning [43], or UCRL [44]. RVI Q-Learning is a model-based RL approach that uses a reference state to bound the state values relative to the value of it. GR-Learning is a model- based algorithm for semi-MDPs that uses the sum of all rewards divided by the time as average reward. Similarly to GR-Learning is UCRL as it is model-based, accumulates the reward and learns the transition probabilities. However, it is only able to infer gain-optimal policies, i.e., policies that optimize for the average reward. Bias values are not considered. (See Sect. 4 for further details.) For a more comprehensive summary of these algorithms see [45]. They also establish a new average reward RL algorithm, called CSV-Learning, where the average reward of the problem has to be predetermined by the user. 4 Foundations of ARAL
Like Miller and Veinott [32] we are concerned with problems that are observed in a sequence of points in time labeled 0; 1; 2; . . . and can be modeled using a finite set of states S, labeled 1; 2; . . .; jSj. At each point t in time the system is in a state st 2 S and by choosing an action at, of a finite set of possible actions As, the system returns a reward rt 1⁄4 rðst; atÞ and transitions to another state stþ1 2 S at time t þ 1 with conditional probability pðstþ1; rt j st; atÞ. Hence, we expect the system to possess the Markov property [1, p.63]. RL processes that possess the Markov property are referred to as Markov decision processes (MDPs) [1, p.66]. Terminal states are absorbing states and are followed by a reset of the system, which starts a new episode [1, p.58]. Recurrent states are revisited with probability 1 [4]. States that are not recurrent are called transient. For periodic states the greatest common divisor of all path lengths to itself is greater than 1. A state that is not periodic is termed aperiodic. A MDPs and its transition probability matrix are called aperiodic if every state is aperiodic, otherwise the MDP is periodic.

5 Discounted and average reward reinforcement learning revisited
We identify four major issues of standard discounted RL for MDPs with nonzero average reward per step. This is partly motivated by similar criticisms by Schwartz and Mahadevan, cf. [4, 15].7
1. Standard discounted RL infers suboptimal policies due to the discount factor being strictly less than one, i.e. c\1. 2. With standard discounted RL it is very difficult to specify a desired balance between short-term and long- term rewards. 3. The average reward per step in the decomposed state value of terminal states is ignored as there are no future states. This leads to poor policies, even when converged. 4. The average reward per step is independently assessed for each state, even though this part of the state value is shared between more than one or, for unichain MPDs, all states. Alas, the issue with Average Reward RL is, that finding the exact solutions are necessary, due to the nested con- straints. Unfortunately, this is very tedious for large state spaces, especially in an iterative manner, as RL is. For instance, if we are interested in correct bias values in an unichain MDP with N states, at least 2N þ 1 nested con- straints have to be solved. The combination of nested constraints and the iterative solution approach have a negative effect on the number of learning steps, as every change on one constraint level affects all consecutive constraint levels. Therefore, it is rather expensive to find the correct values of e.g. VpðsÞ directly. Thus, while favorable in theory, Average Reward RL methodologies are in practice only feasible on very small problems, as bias-optimality is expensive to compute due to the number of constraints and the cyclic interdependencies between constraint levels. The latter is necessary to prevent the accumulation of deviations in the last constraint level, which are caused by the iterative solution approach, cf. Equations 2ff.
In sum, for problems for which the average reward per step cannot be approximated with zero, separately model- ing the average reward is a necessity. Nonetheless, the Average Reward RL idea of solving several nested con- straints, where at least three levels are generally required for bias-optimal policies, directly leads to very long training times. Furthermore, there are only bias-optimal average reward RL algorithms available. Hence, Average Reward RL is no remedy.

6.3 Optimality criteria
In the Literature there are mainly two solution strategies to RL. On the one hand, a single discounted state value is used, while on the other, the decomposition of the state value into infinitely many addends is proposed. The former may lead, as discussed above, to suboptimal policies, while the latter in general incorporates solving infinitely many constraints. We introduce the following definition that delineates a class of algorithms that approximates Black- well-optimality.
Definition 6 If an algorithm A infers for any MDP bias- optimal policies and, for any given MDP, can in theory be configured to infer 1-discount-optimal policies, while 1- discount-optimality is in practice not attainable (for example, as the discount factor can only be chosen cor- rectly in knowledge of the ground truth), we call A near- Blackwell-optimal. Similarly, a Blackwell-optimal policy, inferred by a near-Blackwell-optimal algorithm is called near-Blackwell-optimal.
This definition is of practical relevance, as it defines a group of algorithms that are by far less computationally expensive in comparison to ones that solve infinitely many constraints, but are able to deduce sufficiently optimal policies.

8.3 Cart pole balancing
This commonly-known problem was first described in [54] and is composed of a two-dimensional cart problem, that has a rigid pole attached to it, cf. Figure 8. The agent can apply an impulsive ‘‘right’’ or ‘‘left’’ force F of fixed magnitude to the cart direction on every decision point, changes the cart position x by moving it back-and-forth within certain bounds. The pole is free to move in the vertical plane of the cart and track only. We use the same parameterisation for the simulation as specified in [54], and as used by the gymnasium implementation. As the latter, we use the corrected simulation equations [55]. We do not implement a maximum number of steps per episode, allowing the agent to hypothetically balance the pole for- ever. The episode ends when the pole has reached an inclination of 12 degrees from the center in any direction.
The system state is defined as a quadruple, containing the position x, the angle of the pole with the vertical h, the cart velocity and the rate of change of the angle. As these are continuous values, we discretize them the bounded values (x and h) by scaling with min-max to 1⁄25; 5 and rounding to the nearest integer. For the other two state values we directly round to the closest integer value and clamp those to the same bounds. The original reward function is to return 1 for any step, except for the termi- nating step of the episode, which returns value 0. Hence, with this reward function the average reward is almost exactly 1 and cannot be optimized by the agent. In other words, this reward function reduces the optimisation problem to optimize for the highest error term, while the average reward and the bias values are (almost always) equal, cf. Definition 3 and Equation (1).
Therefore, we have adapted the reward function to include gradual information by providing the maximum angle subtracted by the absolute value of the current angle (both in degrees), i.e. 12  jhj, as reward feedback on every step. For the algorithm setup we use the same values as in the gridworld experiment.
8.4 Mountain car
The Mountain Car MDP [56, p.4-4] consists of a car that is stochastically placed at the bottom of a sinus-shaped mountain. The only way for the agent to steer the car to the upright corner, where the goal is located, is to change the acceleration. It can choose to accelerate to the left, right or not accelerate in every decision point. The parameterisa- tion is set in a way that simply accelerating to the right in order to reach the goal is not possible. Hence, the agent has to learn to swing back-and-forth in the valley until enough momentum is collected to be able to reach the goal. When the goal is reached the episode ends and the environment is reset. The simulation is based on the gymnasium imple- mentation, where we have dropped the maximum number of steps per episode.
The simulated state information consists of two con- tinuous values. First, the current position on the x-axis (2 1⁄21:2; 0:6), with the minimum height being at the center x 1⁄4 0:5, and the velocity of the car 2 1⁄20:07; 0:07. We discretize the position by scaling with min-max to 1⁄25; 5 and rounding to the nearest integer and, in order to reduce the state space, only provide the carts’ direction. We chose this discretization function to provide sufficient information to the agents, but are aware that these are not optimal. The original reward function returns 1 for each step, except for the step terminating the environment, which returns reward 0. Hence, it does not provide intermediate feedback on the progress. Therefore, especially in the tabular case and with discretized state spaces, the problem is hard to solve, requires well-elected parameters, and still often results in policies that do not find the goal in many cases. With the original reward function, the average reward is predefined to a value very close to 1, making it difficult for the agent to find the goal without incremental feedback. Therefore, we changed the reward function as follows. As a default reward 10 is returned on every step, except (i) for the terminating one, which returns 10, and (ii) when moving up the slopes in either of the directions. That is, if the car position is right of the center, i.e. x [  0:5 and has positive velocity (mov- ing right), or if the car position is left of the center (\  0:5) and has negative velocity, the returned reward is computed by the normalized height scaled to the interval ð10; 10Þ. More precisely, it is defined as ð10 þ 20 heightheightmin
heightmaxheightminÞ, where height is the current height of the car. This reward function guides the agent closer to the target, while optimising for the quickest route to the goal. The idea is to (a) enforce moving up to collect momentum and approaching the target, while (b) ensuring that having to go back down results in an overall negative reward and, hence, making the agent to aim for reaching

9.6 Cart pole balancing
As the cart pole balancing task consists of applying left and right impulsive forces to a two-dimensional cart with a rigid pole, the aim is to maintain the pole balanced as long as possible. Hence, the longer the episode, the better. Likewise, as the reward function measures the absolute deviation of the angle of the pole with the vertical sub- tracted from the constant 12 (i.e. the max. deviation), the higher the mean sum of rewards, the better.
Table 9 presents the results. It can be seen that all Q- Learning variants struggle with the example. The best Q- Learning policy is found with a discount factor of 0.5, which can balance the pole for 63.424 steps per episode. This also manifests in a higher mean sum of rewards. The other two variants achieve just over 53 steps. The standard deviations of the average steps per episode are very small, indicating that Q-Learning repeatedly finds far-from-opti- mal policies. In contrast to that, the average reward learning methods, i.e. R-Learning and ARAL, perform much better. They find, on average, policies with 396.606 (ARAL c1 1⁄4 1:0), 453.102 (R-Learning), 489.724 (ARAL c1 1⁄4 0:99), and 678.555 (ARAL c1 1⁄4 0:999) steps before termination. 10 Conclusion and future work
In this work, we focus on such problems that produce an average reward per step that cannot be approximated by 0. We introduce ARAL, a novel adaption of the discounted RL framework and give ample evidence of the usefulness of ARAL in this context. The algorithm is specifically designed for commonly-used unichain (and thus ergodic) MDPs. ARAL explicitly handles the average reward per step, which is used to adjust the discounted state values. Using two different discount factors, the agent infers bias- optimal policies and for any given MDP can be configured to infer Blackwell-optimal policies. We compare ARAL to competing approaches and give ample evidence of its algorithmic effectivity. In the future we plan to use neural networks for function approximation (cf. [12]). Adding to this we plan to investigate the further adaption to an actor- critic version of ARAL.
